title: Leah's sons (Genesis 29:31–35)
hookLine: the unloved sister names each son for a hope, and at Judah simply praises

cards: Put yourself in Leah's place. You were married off in the dark, as a trick. Your husband woke up angry to see your face.
A week later he married your younger sister, the one he really wanted. You live in the same camp, and everyone knows. The Torah says it plainly: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then, in the old JPS translation: "And the LORD saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb." Hated there means loved less, passed over. Nobody in the family seems to see her.
But God sees her. And Leah, the sister nobody chose, starts to have children, and gives each one a name that says exactly what's in her heart.

teach.b: Her first son is Reuben. The name sounds like see, a son, and Leah explains it: God has seen my suffering; now my husband will love me.
The second is Simeon, from the word for hearing: God has heard that I am unloved. The third is Levi, from the word for joining: this time my husband will be joined to me. Seen.
Heard. Joined. Every name is a hope, and every hope is about Jacob.
Maybe this baby will make him love me. And this one. And this one.
It's the tiredness of trying to earn someone's love. Then comes the fourth son, and this time the name is different. "This time will I praise the LORD."
She calls him Judah, Yehudah, from the Hebrew for thanks and praise. No mention of Jacob, or of what she still doesn't have. Just praise.

The Talmud says something startling about this moment: from the day God created the world, no one had ever thanked God, until Leah came and said, this time I will praise. And the story reaches all the way to today.
From Judah comes the tribe of Judah, and from Judah comes the word Jew.

teach.h: THIS TIME WILL I PRAISE THE LORD.
teach.b: The very name of the Jewish people carries Leah's thank-you inside it. The same root opens the short prayer said on waking in Jewish tradition: modeh ani, I give thanks. The unloved sister named the people.
And in the end, it's Leah, not Rachel, who is buried beside Jacob.

how: Jewish tradition begins the morning with Modeh Ani, a short prayer of thanks said on waking, from the same Hebrew root as Judah's name; the word Jew itself comes from Judah.

o: the twelve tribes, all born to one mother
sons named for their father's victories
four names that turn from hoping into praise

games.q: what's inside the names — tap the pairs.
p: my husband will be joined to me

s: every one of Leah's first four sons is named for a hope about Jacob
the first three are. at Judah she stops asking and simply praises.
the word Jew comes from Judah, Leah's fourth son
from Yehudah, whose name means praise, or thanks.
the Talmud says Leah was the first person to thank God
Berakhot 7b: no one thanked God until Leah said, this time I will praise.

games.q: you're Leah. you've named three sons for the hope that your husband will love you. now a fourth is born. what do you name him?
o: another hope: now he'll love me.
praise: this time I will praise the LORD.
games.why: she names him Judah: this time will I praise the LORD. from his name comes the word Jew.

practice: Notice how much of your inner voice is asking, for more time, more money, more love, more rest; that's human, and Leah asked three times.

Now stop asking for a moment, find one thing that is already good, your breath, a person, a meal, a bed tonight, and say thank you with nothing added: no but, no and also. If you pray, you can offer that thanks as your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Leah's sons. Seen, heard, joined, and then Judah: this time, praise. The name the Jewish people still carry.

orig.note: Hebrew: Judah, from the root for thanks and praise. the source of the word Jew.

carryVoice: Your line: this time, praise. Three hopes for love, then one plain thank-you. See you tomorrow.
